items.summary: Morocco staged a comeback from two goals down to secure a late draw against China, keeping their hopes of advancing alive ahead of a decisive match with Group H leaders Spain. Coach Ahmed Kantari praised his players' resilience and focus throughout the game, stating that they deserved the result despite conceding early. A Moroccan player also credited the supporters for helping the team perform well. Morocco now require at least a draw against Spain to guarantee their place in the round of 32.
items.title: Crucial Draw Sets Up Decisive Morocco–Spain Showdown

items.summary: The Guardian interviewed experts across aviation, banking, and national security fields about how AI and other threats are jeopardizing critical infrastructure following a series of recent system disruptions. In the weeks leading up to these interviews, there had been grounded flights, crashing bank websites, Microsoft Outlook outages halting business operations, and hacked sites for Zoom, Ikea, and PokerStars, prompting public speculation about coordinated cyber-attacks by Iranian hackers or autonomous AI agents targeting air traffic control and banking systems.
items.title: Experts Assess Risks to Critical Infrastructure After Recent Mass Outages

items.summary: The COP31 climate conference in Turkey became the longest UN climate talks in history over the weekend, but negotiations failed to produce a deal after the European Union and several countries rejected a final proposal due to its omission of fossil fuels. The breakdown has fueled growing frustration across Europe and raised questions about whether the international climate diplomacy process can still deliver meaningful results or has reached a breaking point. Euronews' Felicia Pochhammer interviewed Chiara Martinelli, director of Climate Action Network, on Europe Tonight to examine what went wrong at the talks in Turkey and what the failed negotiations mean for Europe and the future of global climate action.
items.title: COP31 Talks Fail as EU Rejects Deal Over Fossil Fuel Omission

items.summary: On Monday, Ukraine claimed it was responsible for strikes on two Russian vessels off the coast of Libya, including an attack that sank a modern warship. The attacks occurred Sunday near the Libyan port of Benghazi and represent the latest spillover from Russia's invasion of Ukraine. This comes as Ukraine has increased its daring long-range strikes against targets far from the frontlines in retaliation for Moscow's deadly invasion.
items.title: Ukraine Claims It Sank Russian Warship Off Libya

items.summary: An essay published in The Humanist Review of AI argues that artificial intelligence generates consumer welfare gains through increased product customization and variety, which are not captured by standard quality-based adjustments to gross domestic product. According to the author, new or newly available customized products typically produce larger welfare gains than established products: because such products were previously unavailable—effectively carrying an infinite price for consumers—they become accessible at normal prices when introduced, representing a substantial effective price decline that can be especially large if the consumer values the product highly. The essay notes that comparable gains are harder to achieve by simply purchasing more of an existing product already available over time.
items.title: Essay Argues AI's Product Customization Gains Are Missed by GDP

items.summary: Disguised test vehicles of Hyundai's third-generation Kona have been spotted in the US, Europe, and South Korea over recent months. The new model appears to skip the typical mid-cycle refresh that followed the 2023 second-generation launch, instead receiving a complete redesign with a higher stance and more commanding SUV-like shape similar to the Santa Fe, Palisade, and Tucson. Two versions have been captured: a standard Kona and a rugged XRT variant. For the first time, HealerTV spotted the new Kona N Line in Korea on a car carrier; because it is covered and an early-stage prototype, only exclusive wheels and added lower side skirts are clearly visible, though other N Line design elements such as more aggressive front and rear bumpers are expected. The sighting suggests Hyundai will keep the N Line trim in the third-gen lineup. The new Kona is expected to debut in 2027 as a 2028 model year and be available in gas, hybrid, and fully electric powertrains like the current generation; earlier this month a prototype believed to be the EV version was captured in Korea. Hyundai skipped the 2026 Kona Electric in the US but said it would return for the 2027 model year when the third-generation model arrives.
items.title: Hyundai Spotted Testing New Third-Generation Kona N Line Prototype

items.summary: At the FIFA U-17 World Cup in Doha, Qatar, Mali's under-17 team came from behind to defeat Belgium 2-1. Belgium took an early lead with a goal in the 13th minute, but Djiguo Koita equalized five minutes later at the 18-minute mark. Yaya Niang then scored the winning goal in the second half, completing the comeback for Mali's Young Eagles.
items.title: Mali Beat Belgium 2-1 to Strengthen Under-17 World Cup Qualification Hopes

items.summary:
In South Africa's Limpopo province, residents are still recovering from the January floods that exposed weaknesses in infrastructure and prompted concerns about preparedness for the upcoming rainy season. The January flooding damaged roads, bridges, and water systems across the region, leaving communities to contend with ongoing damage months later while looking ahead uncertainly toward future rains.

In Boelang village, located about 15 kilometers (9.3 miles) southwest of Ba-Phalaborwa in Limpopo's Mopani district, residents had gone without municipal water for almost three months after two main pipelines crossing the Selati River were washed away and a pump station failed. Repairs completed in March restored their water supply, but resident Shanine noted that water pressure remained unreliable with water sometimes flowing slowly. She expressed uncertainty about whether the repaired infrastructure could withstand another flood, pointing out that the community's water system sits directly in the Selati River.

The January floods left a trail of destruction across Limpopo, disrupting learners from attending school and severely damaging water infrastructure. In Ba-Phalaborwa town, residents were placed on a water-shedding schedule as flooding washed away the infrastructure supplying their water supply. Trevor van Rooyen, vice chairperson of the Let's Change Ba-Phalaborwa Community Forum, told Mongabay that he did not believe the government was adequately prepared for further flooding, noting that while damaged roads were patched and bridges destroyed are still under construction.

The damage extended beyond Ba-Phalaborwa. About 170 km away in Tshikunda village under Thulamela municipality, part of a road was washed away in January; by mid-November when Mongabay visited, motorists had created an alternative route through the damaged section that was too narrow for two vehicles to pass simultaneously. Residents of Tshikunda and nearby Tshitereke village are calling on the Limpopo Department of Public Works to urgently repair the Tshikunda bypass road D3681, which links their villages to local schools and Donald Fraser Hospital.

Emmanuel Mongwe, spokesperson for the Limpopo Department of Public Works, Roads and Infrastructure, said work was being finalized on the Tshikunda bypass road as an interim measure while appointing a contractor, with that process expected to be completed by end of November after which construction would resume. Regarding the damaged Selati River bridge, Mongwe said it falls under South African National Roads Agency (SANRAL) responsibility and the department is receiving updates on repair work.

Tsakani Baloyi, director of communications for the Limpopo Department of Cooperative Governance, Human Settlements and Traditional Affairs, told Mongabay that the department had purchased temporary residential units worth 53 million rand ($3 million) to house residents whose homes may be destroyed by rains expected in January 2027. The units were distributed across the province's five districts: Vhembe, Capricorn, Mopani, Waterberg and Sekhukhune, with blankets also available for distribution.

Hope Magidimisha, a national planning commissioner in the Office of the Presidency, said disaster preparedness must begin long before heavy rains arrive. She emphasized identifying vulnerable communities and infrastructure—settlements near rivers, streams and flood lines as well as roads, bridges, schools and other public facilities—and called for greater attention to drainage systems including regular inspections and maintenance before the rainy season.

Magidimisha stressed that early-warning systems are a priority: weather warnings must reach communities in time and in languages people understand so they know what to do when issued. She said an early warning is only useful if it leads to early action, noting it is not enough for the South African Weather Service to issue warnings.

Magidimisha also called for the government to consider long-term solutions including relocation where settlements are situated in dangerous locations, acknowledging this is difficult because people have homes, livelihoods and community connections. She said preparedness should be assessed regularly—identifying vulnerable areas, clearing drainage systems, preparing evacuation plans, ensuring emergency teams are ready and repairing damaged roads and bridges—and that the measure of success should be whether communities are safer rather than money spent or meetings held.

She advised residents to know whether they live in flood-prone areas, where to go during an emergency and whom to contact when their lives or property are threatened, with community leaders involved in preparedness planning particularly for older people, children and people with disabilities. Magidimisha said effective flood preparedness depends on disaster management structures, infrastructure departments, municipalities and communities working together.
items.title: Limpopo Residents Worry About Next Flood After January Damage

items.summary: Analysts at Boston Consulting Group (BCG) said in a September analysis that if quantum-enabled advances in materials, chemistry, and industrial processes reach commercial scale, implications could extend far beyond emissions savings—potentially transforming electricity generation and storage, food production, and carbon removal. BCG experts noted quantum computers are currently better than classical computing and AI at simulating how molecules and materials behave, which could help discover new materials, compounds, battery chemistries, or catalysts for cleaner energy in sectors where renewables cannot reduce the carbon footprint—such as steel-making, cement, aluminum, chemicals, shipping, and aviation. BCG added that breakthrough battery chemistries discovered with quantum modeling could accelerate electrification rates globally by potentially making electricity cheaper and more accessible, but major quantum-driven changes and significant emissions reductions could be years away depending on scaling.
items.title: Quantum Computing Could Accelerate the Energy Transition

items.summary: Noelia Ordieres Buarfa-Mohamed, a 41-year-old climber from Llanes who was recovering from a broken right leg sustained training on an indoor climbing wall — two operations, six months in a wheelchair, and sixteen screws later — climbed to the summit of Lenin Peak at the Kyrgyzstan–Tajikistan border. She reached the Edelweiss meadow where eight Soviet climbers are buried there but found no signage, marked trail, or plaque; she said their names aloud out loud and decided to tell their story.
items.title: Climber retraces the fatal descent of the first all-female team to Lenin Peak
